 Full battery lasts (fridge only) 2.4 days 
 Per week 3 kWh 
 Show calculation 1 Energy: 45 W × 24 h × 40% = 432 Wh/day 
 2 Equals: 432 Wh ÷ 12.8 V = 33.8 Ah/day 
 3 Battery runtime: 100 Ah × 12.8 V × 80% ÷ 432 Wh/day = 2.4 days 
 Copy result Copy link 
 How it's calculated
 Compressor refrigerators cycle via thermostat: the rated power is only drawn during run phases. Consumption therefore depends on the duty cycle – and that on ambient temperature, insulation, how full it is and door openings.
 Energy [Wh/day] = rated power [W] × 24 h × duty cycle 45 W × 24 h × 40% = 432 Wh Absorption refrigerators produce cold from heat – from propane, a 12 V heating element or 120 V AC. On propane the consumption in g/h (or BTU/h) per the data sheet counts; on 12 V the heating element runs continuously without a thermostat (only while driving), on 120 V it cycles.
 Propane [g/day] = consumption [g/h] × operating hours
12 V: energy = heating element [W] × driving hours
120 V: energy = heating element [W] × hours × duty cycle Thermoelectric coolers (Peltier) run continuously and only reach about 27–36 °F (15–20 °C) below ambient temperature.
 Battery runtime [days] = capacity [Ah] × voltage [V] × usable fraction ÷ energy per day 
 Worked example
 A 3.2 cu ft (90 L) compressor fridge rated at 50 W runs about 50% of the time at 82 °F (28 °C); the house battery is a 100 Ah LiFePO4 with 80% usable.
 Inputs
 Refrigerator type: Compressor refrigerator (12 V)
 Power draw: 50 W
 Operating hours per day: 24 h
 Duty cycle (thermostat): 50 %
 Battery capacity: 100 Ah
 Usable fraction: 80 %
 System voltage: 12 V LiFePO4 (12.8 V)
 Result
 600 Wh
 Power consumption per day
 Equals 46.9 Ah/day 
 Full battery lasts (fridge only) 1.7 days 
 Per week 4.2 kWh 
 Calculation
 Energy: 50 W × 24 h × 50% = 600 Wh/day
 Equals: 600 Wh ÷ 12.8 V = 46.9 Ah/day
 Battery runtime: 100 Ah × 12.8 V × 80% ÷ 600 Wh/day = 1.7 days
 The variables explained
 Power draw (W) Per the nameplate. Compressor 40–60 W, absorption heating element 12 V 120–170 W, 120 V 125–190 W. 
 Propane consumption (g/h) Per the absorption fridge's data sheet; 14–18 g/h (≈ 670–860 BTU/h) is typical for 3–3.5 cu ft (80–100 L). 
 Duty cycle (%) Run-time share of the compressor or the 120 V heating element. 30% at 68 °F (20 °C), 50% at 86 °F (30 °C), up to 70% in high summer. 
 Operating hours (h) 24 h when parked; for 12 V absorption fridges the daily driving time. 
 Common mistakes
 Calculating a compressor fridge at rated power × 24 h – that overestimates consumption two- to threefold. 
 Running an absorption fridge on 12 V while parked: 130 W without a thermostat drains a 100 Ah battery in less than a day. 
 Neglecting ventilation: blocked vents or sun on the fridge wall raise the duty cycle considerably. 
 Underestimating freezing supplies: a freezer compartment in use can double consumption. 
 Assumptions and limits
 Constant duty cycle over the day; at night the compressor usually runs less often.
 Typical consumption values per manufacturer data (Dometic, Thetford) – your own data sheet takes precedence.
 Absorption fridges on propane additionally need a few Wh per day for control and ignition (neglected).
 Frequently asked questions
 How long does a 100 Ah battery last with a compressor fridge? At 430 Wh daily consumption and 1,024 Wh usable energy (LiFePO4, 80%) about 2.4 days – with no other loads. With an AGM (600 Wh usable) about 1.4 days.
 Absorption or compressor – which is more economical? Parked without shore power, the absorption fridge on propane uses practically no electricity and needs 0.7–1 lb (300–450 g) of propane a day. The compressor needs 300–600 Wh of electricity but also cools reliably in heat and when not level. With a solar system the compressor is usually the better choice today.

What Size Power Station for a 12V Fridge? 400-550Wh a Day | Volt & Valley 
 Volt & Valley is reader-funded. We earn a commission when you buy through our links, at no extra cost to you, as an Amazon Associate. Commission never decides a ranking — see how we choose and our affiliate disclosure .
 The short answer
 A 12V compressor fridge typically uses 400-550 watt-hours a day — roughly a third of a full-size household refrigerator — because it draws 40-60W only while the compressor is running, which is 30-50% of the time. That means a 286-288Wh unit covers most of a day, a 1,024Wh unit covers about two days, and a 2,048Wh unit covers about four. Run the fridge from the power station's 12V socket rather than through the AC inverter and you save another 15-20% on top.

 Our pick
 EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus

 Read the full review first → 
 This is the most commonly over-sized purchase on the site, and it happens for a specific reason: people read the household-refrigerator figure, apply it to a camping fridge, and buy three times the unit they need. A 12V compressor fridge and a kitchen refrigerator are different appliances with different physics, and the gap between them is about 800Wh a day. 
 Why a 12V fridge is so much cheaper to run
 It is smaller. 40-75 litres against 400-600 litres of cabinet to keep cold. 
 It is better insulated for its size. A camping fridge is built to hold temperature in a hot car, which is a harder brief than a kitchen appliance faces. 
 It has a DC compressor. No inverter in the path when you run it from a 12V socket, which removes the 15-20% conversion loss a household fridge on a power station always pays. 
 It cycles less in cool conditions. A fridge in a shaded van at 70F has a much lower duty cycle than the same fridge in a 100F car. 
 The exception worth naming is a thermoelectric or Peltier cooler, which is a completely different device despite looking similar. Those draw continuously rather than cycling, and they are far more expensive to run than a compressor fridge of the same size. If your cooler has no compressor, every figure on this page is optimistic — check which type you own. 
 The arithmetic
 Daily watt-hours, and days of runtime
 Daily Wh = running watts x 24 x duty cycle 
 A 45W fridge at 40%: 45 x 24 x 0.4 = 432Wh a day 
 The same fridge in a hot car at 60%: 45 x 24 x 0.6 = 648Wh a day 
 On DC, no inverter loss: 432Wh of battery for 432Wh of fridge 
 Through the AC inverter, add 18%: 432 / 0.85 = about 508Wh of battery 
 Days on 1,024Wh via DC: 1024 / 432 = about 2.4 days 
 Days on 1,024Wh via AC: 1024 / 508 = about 2.0 days 
 Running the fridge on DC buys you roughly an extra half-day per kilowatt-hour of battery, for free. It is the single easiest saving in this whole category. 
 Read the plate on your own fridge for its running wattage, and then be honest about the duty cycle you will actually see. Ambient temperature is the biggest variable by a wide margin, and the figures above are a worked example rather than a measurement of your appliance. How many watt-hours does a refrigerator use covers how to measure a duty cycle properly if you want your own number. 
 The sizing table
 Capacity against 12V fridge days, using a 432Wh daily figure on DC. Substitute your own fridge's number. Capacity Days of fridge only Plus phones and lights Verdict 
 286-288Wh About 0.6 days Half a day A long day trip 
 1,024-1,152Wh 2.4-2.7 days About 2 days A weekend 
 2,048Wh About 4.7 days 3-4 days A long weekend or a week with solar 
 3,840-4,096Wh 8-9 days 6-7 days Off-grid, with panels 
 For most people the honest answer is the 1kWh class: two days of fridge with the phones, lights and a laptop evening alongside, and a weekend is the trip most people actually take. If your trips are longer, the fix is usually a panel rather than a bigger battery — see below. 
 The surge question, which is smaller here
 A 12V compressor still demands more current at start than it does running, but the absolute numbers are far smaller than a household fridge's. Where a 150W kitchen fridge can ask for 600-1,200W at start-up, a 45W camping fridge's inrush sits well inside the smallest inverters here. That is why a 286Wh unit with 600W of continuous output runs one without complaint, where the same unit cannot start a kitchen refrigerator at all. Can a power station run a refrigerator covers the household case where surge genuinely decides it. 
 Solar makes this load disappear
 A 12V fridge is the one significant load that a single portable panel can genuinely cover. A 200W panel at five peak sun hours and a 0.75 derate delivers roughly 750Wh a day, against a 432Wh fridge — which means in reasonable sun the fridge runs indefinitely and the surplus charges everything else. 
 That is the reason best solar generator for a refrigerator splits its advice by fridge type: 100-200W of panel for a 12V unit, 400-500W for a household one. How much solar input do you need has the derate reasoning, and how long to charge a power station with solar covers the refill time. 
 Five practical savings
 Run it on DC. The 12V socket rather than the AC inverter. Worth 15-20% for nothing. 
 Keep it out of the sun. Ambient temperature drives the duty cycle more than any setting does. 
 Pre-chill at home. Arrive with the fridge and its contents already cold and the first day's draw drops sharply. 
 Fill it. A full fridge holds temperature between compressor cycles; a half-empty one cycles more. 
 Open it less. Every opening dumps cold air, and on a 40 litre box that is a meaningful fraction of the contents. 
 Which unit, and where this fits
 For a weekend with a fridge, best power station for a camping fridge is the commercial shortlist built on exactly this arithmetic. For a van where the fridge runs permanently, what size power station for van life adds the rest of the build — and once a diesel heater, lights and a water pump are in the total, the fridge is still the biggest single line. 
 On a boat the same numbers apply with a weather caveat: best power station for a boat notes that no unit in this registry publishes a water-ingress rating, so the battery has to live somewhere dry even though the fridge does not. 
 What we have not done
 We have not metered a 12V fridge, and the 40-60W and 30-50% duty-cycle figures are category bands rather than measurements of your appliance — read your own plate and, if the purchase is large, measure a day with an energy meter.  Questions
 Frequently asked questions
 What size power station do I need for a 12V fridge? + The 1kWh class for a weekend. A 12V compressor fridge typically uses 400-550Wh a day, so a 1,024Wh unit covers about two days of fridge with phones and lights alongside, a 286Wh unit covers most of a long day, and 2,048Wh covers four to five days. 
 How many watt-hours does a 12V fridge use per day? + Typically 400-550Wh, because it draws 40-60W only while the compressor runs, which is 30-50% of the time. Multiply your fridge's plate wattage by 24 and by your realistic duty cycle to get your own figure — ambient temperature is the biggest variable. 
 Should I run a 12V fridge from the AC outlet or the 12V socket? + The 12V socket. A DC compressor fridge run through the AC inverter pays a 15-20% conversion loss for nothing, which is roughly half a day of extra runtime per kilowatt-hour of battery that you simply give away. 
 Why does a 12V fridge use so much less than a household fridge? + It is a tenth of the cabinet volume, better insulated for its size, and it runs a DC compressor with no inverter in the path. A full-size kitchen refrigerator is roughly 1,000-1,500Wh a day against a 12V fridge's 400-550Wh. 
 Can a 300W power station run a 12V fridge? + Yes — the output requirement is modest because a 45W compressor's inrush sits well inside even a small inverter. The limit is capacity rather than output: a 286-288Wh unit is most of a day, not a weekend. 
 Will one solar panel keep a 12V fridge running? + In reasonable sun, yes. A 200W panel at five peak sun hours and a realistic 0.75 derate delivers about 750Wh a day against a 432Wh fridge, which leaves surplus for phones and lights. This is the one significant load a single portable panel genuinely covers.
